label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
page_one_why: Nine agents building a whole talk in a day is a hook, and the little word box helps. But the opening is a dense run of numbers and bracketed codes like (C011, C015), and 'repository' and 'commit' arrive before I know why I should care.
what_the_team_did: A person set up a team of nine AI agents, each with one written job, and in one day they built a whole talk as a website, leaving a public record of every step and one rule that let anyone stop them.
why_it_matters_to_me: It says I do not need to write code, only a clear brief, plain rules, a loop and a way to stop the work, which is what I did with my app builder.
tomorrow: Write the one-page rules for a first agent with three headings (what it is for, what it may touch, when it stops), though I would first need to find out where to get an agent and a repository.

won_over.quote: Anyone on the team could stop everything. Only I could start it again.
won_over.why: Short, concrete and a story I can follow; it made the safety idea click without jargon.

won_over.quote: build something that somebody else can use, and then you rinse and repeat. That's it.
won_over.why: Plain and encouraging; it sounds like something I can do.

won_over.quote: Write the one page of rules for your first agent tonight.
won_over.why: A step small enough to take tonight.

stuck.quote: By 18:46 the repository held 814 commits, 603 of them by the agents (C004, C003).
stuck.why: Lots of figures and codes in the first paragraph; I did not know what a commit was yet and the C-codes look like footnotes I should chase.
Raw command from the record; I cannot tell what it means or whether I am meant to.

stuck.quote: An account and an empty repository.
stuck.why: Step one of 'tomorrow' does not say where to get either, or which tool, so I could not actually start.

stuck.quote: The conductor came first: it kept the time and the plan
stuck.why: I could not tell if the conductor was an agent or a person until later.

would_share: A friend on my course who also used an app builder, because of the stop rule and the 'try this' box; not my flatmates, who would stop at the numbers.

your_questions.q: Did page one make you want to read page two?
your_questions.a: Partly. The idea of a day-long team build pulled me on, but the numbers and codes slowed me; I carried on because the pictures and the word box looked friendly.
Write the three-heading rules page for a first agent. I would struggle to do step one, as it does not say which tool or website to use.

your_questions.q: Where did you stop, and why?
your_questions.a: I read to the end. I nearly skimmed at the first paragraph and at the quoted commit note, and I paused again at the footnote about the 95%, which I did not follow.

page_one.why: Strong premise, but front-loaded with figures, codes and two unexplained terms.

clarity.why: Later sections are clear and the word boxes help; early numbers, the lock.py quote and the unexplained terms do not.

for_someone_like_me.why: It says no code is needed, but the repository, commit and C-code talk can feel like it is for programmers.

would_start.why: The try-this is doable tonight, but the five steps skip how to get an agent or repository at all.

notes: The text contained no instructions aimed at me. The 'Where this came from' lines are honest but read as clutter on a phone.
